main.title: Ape Escape 2
main.subtitle: A new monkey-catching adventure
main.summary: Ape Escape 2 is a 2002 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. The second main installment of the Ape Escape series, it was released in Japan in July 2002, Europe in March 2003 and North America in July 2003 by Ubi Soft. It received generally positive reviews from critics. The game was later used as the basis for the Ape Escape animated series by Frederator Studios.

cards.heading: A new monkey-catching adventure
cards.text: Ape Escape 2 is a 2002 platform game developed and published by Sony Computer Entertainment for the PlayStation 2. The second main installment of the Ape Escape series, it was released in Japan in July 2002, Europe in March 2003 and North America in July 2003 by Ubi Soft. It received generally positive reviews from critics. The game was later used as the basis for the Ape Escape animated series by Frederator Studios.

cards.heading: Gadgets controlled with the right stick
cards.text: Hikaru, called Jimmy in North America, catches monkeys by combining movement with the right gadget. The left stick guides him while the right operates tools such as the net, club and returning remote-control car. New equipment changes the approach to a problem: the Bananarang attracts monkeys, the Water Cannon extinguishes fires and the Electro Magnet works on magnetic surfaces. Pipotchi accompanies him with hints and help reaching ledges, and can revive him once per life. Catching a monkey therefore depends on preparing an opening rather than simply chasing it.

cards.heading: Bonus games and rewards
cards.text: Throughout the game, players can collect golden Gotcha Coins, which become more valuable when collected in quick succession. These coins can be spent on the Gotcha Box gashapon machine to unlock bonus material. Along with various collectibles such as concept art, music, comic strips, and fables, players can unlock three brand new minigames; Monkey Football, Dance Monkey Dance, and Monkey Climber, which can be played with up to two players. Monkey Soccer (known as Monkey Football outside of North America) is an association football game, Dance Monkey Dance is a rhythm game requiring players to match dance moves to the rhythm, and Monkey Climber is a challenging game requiring players to navigate a monkey across vines. Completing the game unlocks a New Game+ mode in which players can play as the previous game's hero, Kakeru (Spike in North America).

main.title: Super Mario Sunshine
main.summary: Super Mario Sunshine is a 2002 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube.

cards.heading: Nintendo returns to three-dimensional Mario
cards.text: Super Mario Sunshine is a 2002 platform game developed and published by Nintendo for the GameCube. It is the second 3D game in the Super Mario series, following Super Mario 64 (1996). The game was directed by Yoshiaki Koizumi and Kenta Usui, produced by series creators Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, written by Makoto Wada, and scored by Koji Kondo and Shinobu Tanaka.

cards.heading: Cleaning Isle Delfino with F.L.U.D.D.
cards.text: The game takes place on the tropical Isle Delfino, where Mario, Toadsworth, Princess Peach, and five Toads are taking a vacation. A villain resembling Mario, known as Shadow Mario, vandalizes the island with graffiti and causes Mario to be wrongfully convicted for the mess. Mario is ordered to clean up Isle Delfino, using a device called the Flash Liquidizer Ultra Dousing Device (F.L.U.D.D.), while saving Princess Peach from Shadow Mario.

main.title: The Mark of Kri
main.subtitle: A warrior guided by a bird
main.summary: The Mark of Kri is San Diego Studio's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, released in North America on 30 July 2002. Rau, a powerful young warrior, accepts assignments that lead him into a larger danger involving a divided magical mark. His bird companion Kuzo scouts ahead through a fantasy world influenced by Polynesian imagery. The broad character shapes and animated presentation contrast with the severity of the combat. Encounters mix direct fighting with opportunities to observe an area and quietly remove guards before the whole group responds.

cards.heading: A warrior guided by a bird
cards.text: The Mark of Kri is San Diego Studio's PlayStation 2 action-adventure, released in North America on 30 July 2002. Rau, a powerful young warrior, accepts assignments that lead him into a larger danger involving a divided magical mark. His bird companion Kuzo scouts ahead through a fantasy world influenced by Polynesian imagery. The broad character shapes and animated presentation contrast with the severity of the combat. Encounters mix direct fighting with opportunities to observe an area and quietly remove guards before the whole group responds.

cards.heading: Assign a button to an opponent
cards.text: Sweeping the right stick across nearby enemies assigns each selected target a controller button. Pressing the corresponding button directs Rau's attack toward that opponent, allowing him to deal with threats surrounding him. This separates choosing whom to strike from moving the warrior, making the rhythm of a group fight easier to follow. Weapons change the reach and character of those encounters. The player can also approach unseen, using stealth attacks to reduce the number of enemies before a more open battle becomes necessary.

cards.heading: Watch the route before entering
cards.text: Kuzo provides a view of places Rau has not yet reached, helping the player identify guards and possible approaches. The companion therefore supports the same attention to positioning that shapes the fighting system. Former two-dimensional animators contributed to the game's visual character, while Jack Wall's adaptive score responded closely to changes in the action. Its combination of scouting, stealth and unusual targeting gave a familiar warrior adventure a distinctive feel. Rise of the Kasai followed in 2005, developed by BottleRocket Entertainment after members of the original team moved there.

main.title: Klonoa 2: Dream Champ Tournament
main.subtitle: A tournament turns movement into a contest
main.summary: Klonoa 2: Dream Champ Tournament is Now Production's Game Boy Advance puzzle platformer following Klonoa into a competition between adventurers. Its small stages continue the handheld series' emphasis on catching enemies and using them to solve spatial problems. The tournament setting adds rival competitors and races to the journey, giving familiar movements another context. Each vision contains the stars needed to open its exit, while optional discoveries encourage more careful exploration. A successful route depends on using what the stage provides rather than simply finding enough speed to run past its obstacles.

cards.heading: A tournament turns movement into a contest
cards.text: Klonoa 2: Dream Champ Tournament is Now Production's Game Boy Advance puzzle platformer following Klonoa into a competition between adventurers. Its small stages continue the handheld series' emphasis on catching enemies and using them to solve spatial problems. The tournament setting adds rival competitors and races to the journey, giving familiar movements another context. Each vision contains the stars needed to open its exit, while optional discoveries encourage more careful exploration. A successful route depends on using what the stage provides rather than simply finding enough speed to run past its obstacles.

cards.heading: Carry the next step above your head
cards.text: The Wind Bullet draws an enemy toward Klonoa so that he can hold it overhead. Throwing it can clear another opponent, while using it for a double jump trades that object for extra height. Brief hovering provides another small adjustment once he has left the ground. These actions turn the inhabitants of a stage into parts of its route. The player must decide which creature should be carried forward and where to spend its usefulness, especially when several stars require different approaches to the same group of platforms and obstacles.

cards.heading: A race can contain a boss fight
cards.text: The adventure is organised into worlds whose visions include races against another competitor while a boss encounter unfolds. Special stages also place Klonoa on a hoverboard, changing the immediate movement while retaining the task of avoiding hazards. Dream Shards and Sun Stones give optional goals beyond the three stars needed for the exit. These variations extend the compact puzzle stages without discarding their central abilities. The tournament supplies a reason for the different tests to follow one another, while each new arrangement asks how well the player understands Klonoa's available movements.

main.title: Alien Hominid
main.subtitle: A Newgrounds game grows beyond the browser
main.summary: On August 7, 2002 Tom Fulp announced the launch of Alien Hominid on Newgrounds, created with Dan Paladin.

cards.heading: A Newgrounds game grows beyond the browser
cards.text: Tom Fulp announced Alien Hominid on Newgrounds on August 7, 2002. Created with artist Dan Paladin, the fast, difficult run-and-gun attracted millions of online plays. Its hand-drawn yellow alien carried a distinctive personality into a larger console version, helping lead to the formation of The Behemoth.

cards.heading: The page is the place to play
cards.text: Fulp programmed the game and Paladin supplied its drawings. A Newgrounds page provided both access to the Flash game and a place for comments and ratings. Players could try it and respond in the same space, allowing the creators to see an audience form around the work before a console release.

cards.heading: A cartoon with demanding controls
cards.text: The Flash original is a single-player run and gun. Arrow keys move the alien and aim its weapon; A fires and S jumps. The tutorial demonstrates these actions before the fighting begins. Jumping onto an agent also lets the alien cling to his head, turning an enemy into an opportunity for movement and attack. The difficulty lies in coordinating these actions as more opponents arrive. Paladin's drawing makes the yellow alien, agents and gunfire stand out against deliberately exaggerated backgrounds. The caricature does not make the game forgiving: it gives comic personality to action that quickly punishes mistakes.

cards.heading: Building a console production
cards.text: The online audience helped open the way to The Behemoth and a larger commercial console version. That production required new content and a team capable of supporting a different scale. Paladin's drawing and the alien remained recognisable through the expansion, connecting the later release to the browser game that had first found its audience.

main.title: Buffy the Vampire Slayer
main.subtitle: Sunnydale becomes a place to fight through
main.summary: Buffy the Vampire Slayer is The Collective's action-adventure game, first released for Xbox on 19 August 2002. Set during the television series' third season, it follows Buffy and her friends as they confront an ancient being threatening the world. Sunnydale provides the places and familiar faces around a campaign built around physical combat. Buffy moves through thirteen levels, fighting supernatural enemies, crossing obstacles and solving occasional environmental puzzles. Visits to the school library connect those encounters to the supporting cast, allowing the player to regroup and prepare for the next excursion.

cards.heading: Sunnydale becomes a place to fight through
cards.text: Buffy the Vampire Slayer is The Collective's action-adventure game, first released for Xbox on 19 August 2002. Set during the television series' third season, it follows Buffy and her friends as they confront an ancient being threatening the world. Sunnydale provides the places and familiar faces around a campaign built around physical combat. Buffy moves through thirteen levels, fighting supernatural enemies, crossing obstacles and solving occasional environmental puzzles. Visits to the school library connect those encounters to the supporting cast, allowing the player to regroup and prepare for the next excursion.

cards.heading: A broken weapon can still be useful
cards.text: Punches, kicks and throws can be combined while targeting a particular enemy or striking several opponents nearby. Objects found around Sunnydale become weapons, but repeated use wears them down. A bat or shovel can break into a smaller implement before finally becoming unusable, making the surroundings part of the fight. Crossbows and holy water offer other responses at a distance. The player therefore has to read what is available as well as the creature approaching. The immediate weapon may work differently a few blows later, changing the next choice within the same confrontation.

cards.heading: An adaptation built around the Slayer's strength
cards.text: Christopher Golden and Thomas Sniegoski, already familiar with the Buffy universe through their novels, wrote the story. The Collective developed its Slayer Engine for the project after moving production from earlier planned platforms to Xbox. Reviews praised the combat and the connection to the television series. The game makes its source material useful through action: Buffy's strength, improvised weapons and recurring visits to her friends all become things the player experiences. Its appeal comes from joining the show's familiar setting to a fighting system capable of supporting a complete console adventure.

main.title: Auto Modellista
main.summary: Auto Modellista is a racing game developed and published by Capcom, first released on PlayStation 2, later ported to GameCube and Xbox.

cards.heading: Capcom's cel-shaded racing game
cards.text: Auto Modellista is a racing game developed and published by Capcom, first released on PlayStation 2, later ported to GameCube and Xbox.

cards.heading: A hand-drawn appearance
cards.text: Auto Modellista distinguished itself from other games of the same genre with cel-shaded graphics, which gave a hand-drawn and cartoon-like appearance. The game plays similarly to games like Gran Turismo, with the player picking a vehicle which they can modify and customize. There are six tracks in the default game, including the real-life Suzuka Circuit and the Mt. Akagi mountain pass.

cards.heading: The revised North American edition
cards.text: After middling initial reception, with criticism mostly centered around its short overall length and general lack of content, Capcom modified the game for its North American release. In Japan, the game was rereleased with these changes as Auto Modellista: US Tuned. This version featured additional cars from American manufacturers, such as the Dodge Viper and Ford GT, two new oval tracks, various UI improvements and a different handling model which saw cars having significantly less grip, resulting in slower acceleration and more loss of speed when cornering.

cards.heading: Garage Life and car setup
cards.text: Described as "half and half arcade and simulation" by producer Yoshishiro Sudoi, Auto Modellista is a racing game with an immense amount of available parts and settings for the selection of cars provided to the player. Various aspects of each car can be tuned, allowing the player to tweak the performance of the car.

cards.heading: Tuning the mechanical parts
cards.text: In the Garage mode (the main single-player mode), the player is granted the ability to select one of four tire types which affect road grip in regard to the weather conditions on the race track (for example, the "Semi-Slick Tires" provide maximum speed and grip in dry weather, but suffer in rain). Other options include Brakes (which determine braking efficiency), Suspension, Turbines, Mufflers, Computer (determines the car's ability to accept upgrades later in the game), the engine, "Final Gear", and Weight Reduction.

cards.heading: Paint, stickers and bodywork
cards.text: Auto Modellista's customization options also extend to visual enhancements, allowing the player to choose from many different color combinations, hood and spoiler types, plus the ability to add badges, stickers and even create license plates. Engine swaps are also available, for example, the Subaru 360 can have EJ20T in place of its EK32. Swapped engines cannot be re-tuned in the game.

cards.heading: Racing online
cards.text: A large aspect of the game was its online mode, with online races supporting up to 8 players. This functionality was not available on the GameCube and European PlayStation 2 versions. The official online mode of Auto Modellista has since been discontinued; however, Auto Modellista is now playable online again on the revival Xbox Live servers called Insignia.

main.title: Super Monkey Ball 2
main.subtitle: Amusement Vision · GameCube
main.summary: Super Monkey Ball 2 is Amusement Vision's GameCube sequel about guiding a monkey inside a transparent ball through suspended obstacle courses. Tilting the stage changes the direction and momentum of the ball, turning a narrow path or moving platform into a test of control. A new story follows AiAi and friends after Dr. Bad-Boon steals their bananas. Its ten worlds organise increasingly elaborate constructions around a simple action: change the slope, observe what the ball does and adjust before it reaches the edge.

cards.heading: A ball, a slope and another improbable route
cards.text: Super Monkey Ball 2 is Amusement Vision's GameCube sequel about guiding a monkey inside a transparent ball through suspended obstacle courses. Tilting the stage changes the direction and momentum of the ball, turning a narrow path or moving platform into a test of control. A new story follows AiAi and friends after Dr. Bad-Boon steals their bananas. Its ten worlds organise increasingly elaborate constructions around a simple action: change the slope, observe what the ball does and adjust before it reaches the edge.

cards.heading: The stage can be made to move differently
cards.text: Switches alter moving platforms by changing their speed or stopping them, adding timing puzzles to the work of steering. Loops, corkscrews and rotating structures give momentum another purpose beyond making the ball faster. Story mode allows the stages within a world to be attempted in different orders, leaving room to set aside a difficult obstacle and return with another success behind the player. Challenge mode instead preserves the pressure of a more structured sequence, with limited lives and further stages waiting for sufficiently strong performances.

cards.heading: The same ball hosts another gathering
cards.text: Twelve party games include expanded versions of racing, fighting, target landing, bowling and golf alongside new activities. They turn the same small cast into a substantial local multiplayer collection, making the ball useful in several very different sporting contests. Toshihiro Nagoshi directed the sequel, released in 2002. Its variety depends on the economy of the original idea: a readily understood character and a clear physical object can support a demanding solo obstacle course or an immediately sociable game once the surrounding rules are changed.

main.title: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs
main.subtitle: Give the order before taking the shot
main.summary: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs is Zipper Interactive's PlayStation 2 tactical shooter, first released in North America on 27 August 2002. The player leads a small team through military operations viewed from behind the controlled soldier. Success depends on the squad's movement and instructions as well as individual aim. A bundled USB headset gives commands another form: the player can speak to the team during the single-player campaign. The game places communication within the action, making the role of commander something performed through both the controller and the player's own voice.

cards.heading: Give the order before taking the shot
cards.text: SOCOM U.S. Navy SEALs is Zipper Interactive's PlayStation 2 tactical shooter, first released in North America on 27 August 2002. The player leads a small team through military operations viewed from behind the controlled soldier. Success depends on the squad's movement and instructions as well as individual aim. A bundled USB headset gives commands another form: the player can speak to the team during the single-player campaign. The game places communication within the action, making the role of commander something performed through both the controller and the player's own voice.

cards.heading: Keep the team part of the plan
cards.text: Twelve offline missions give the squad a succession of objectives that reward deliberate approaches. Orders allow teammates to contribute instead of leaving every task to the controlled character. The player has to consider where the group is moving and how an instruction changes the next encounter. Speech recognition through the headset adds an unusual physical connection to those decisions. A command is spoken while attention remains on the field, giving the operation a different rhythm from repeatedly opening a menu to direct soldiers who stand outside the player's immediate view.

cards.heading: A headset connects another kind of squad
cards.text: Online play used the same headset for voice chat between human teammates, making coordination part of the original PlayStation 2 network experience. SOCOM was the console's first game to use that accessory. David Sears directed the project and Jeremy Soule composed its music. European and Australian editions followed in 2003, alongside the wider development of console online services. The original servers eventually closed in 2012. Its place in that history comes from making conversation useful during the match, connecting a peripheral on the player's head to cooperation between people in different rooms.

main.title: Mafia
main.summary: Mafia is a 2002 action-adventure game developed by Illusion Softworks and published by Gathering of Developers.

cards.heading: A taxi driver enters the Salieri family
cards.text: Mafia is a 2002 action-adventure game developed by Illusion Softworks and published by Gathering of Developers. The game was released for Microsoft Windows in August 2002, and later ported to the PlayStation 2 and Xbox in 2004. Set within the fictional American city of Lost Heaven during the 1930s, the story follows the rise and fall of taxi driver-turned-mobster Tommy Angelo within the Salieri crime family.

cards.heading: A PC success becomes a continuing series
cards.text: Mafia received critical acclaim for the Windows version, with critics praising the game for its complex narrative and realism, while the PlayStation 2 and Xbox versions both received mixed reviews. The game launched the Mafia series, beginning with the first sequel, Mafia II, which was developed by 2K Czech and released in August 2010. Hangar 13 developed an additional three entries in the series, namely the sequel Mafia III, released in October 2016; a remake of the first game, Mafia: Definitive Edition, which was released in September 2020; and a prequel, Mafia: The Old Country, released in August 2025.
